library(tidyverse)

# Example data
data <- data.frame(
  age = rnorm(100, 50, 10),
  blood_pressure = rnorm(100, 120, 15),
  treatment = sample(c("A", "B"), 100, replace = TRUE)

# Summary statistics

    Welch Two Sample t-test

t = -1.3721, df = 94.534, p-value = 0.1733

sample estimates:
mean in group A mean in group B 
       117.6492        122.0554 



R uses Welch’s t-test by default (does not assume equal variances).
The confidence interval is for the first group minus the second (A − B), so the sign follows the order of the groups.
The sample estimates show each group’s mean.





# paired: the same 30 people before and after
before <- rnorm(30, 140, 12)
after  <- before - rnorm(30, 5, 6)
t.test(before, after, paired = TRUE)


    Paired t-test

data:  before and after
t = 1.4842, df = 29, p-value = 0.1485
alternative hypothesis: true mean difference is not equal to 0
95 percent confidence interval:
 -0.8405802  5.2883927
sample estimates:
mean difference 
       2.223906 

# non-parametric alternative for two independent groups
wilcox.test(blood_pressure ~ treatment, data = data)


    Wilcoxon rank sum test with continuity correction

data:  blood_pressure by treatment
W = 1027, p-value = 0.1556
alternative hypothesis: true location shift is not equal to 0






A p-value says how surprising the data would be if there were no true difference.
It is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and not the probability the result is “due to chance”.
It says nothing about the size or importance of the difference: look at the estimate and its confidence interval.
A large p-value is weak evidence against “no difference”. It is not proof that there is none.

title: Introduction to R
text:
Project: why not setwd()?

A Project (.Rproj) makes its own folder the working directory every time you open it
Paths are then relative to the project: read_csv("data/ncd_survey.csv") works on any computer
setwd("C:/Users/Asha/Desktop") only works on one machine, and breaks when you share the script
Keep raw data in data/, write all steps in a script (not only the console), and never overwrite the raw file

title: Introduction to R
text:
Variables and Data Types

Numeric — numbers such as 3.14, 42
Integer — whole numbers with L suffix, e.g. 5L
Character — text values like "data"
Logical — TRUE or FALSE
Factor — categorical values with levels
Complex — numbers with imaginary parts like 1 + 2i



Show the code
x <- 5          # numeric
name <- "Alice" # character
flag <- TRUE    # logical
colors <- factor(c("red", "blue", "green"))



Variables store values in memory and can be reused later
R is dynamically typed: type depends on the stored value

title: Introduction to R
text:
Vectors and Sequences

Create ordered collections with c() and sequences with seq()
Useful for numeric data, indexes, and repeated values



Show the code
ages <- c(23, 35, 28)
seq(1, 100, 3)
seq(1, 2, length.out = 10)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Factors and Categorical Variables

Store categories or groups with fixed levels
Important for statistical modeling and reporting
Use factor() to make discrete labels or ordered categories



Show the code
gender <- factor(c("Male", "Female", "Male", "Female"),
                 levels = c("Male", "Female"))
physical_activity <- factor(sample(c(1, 2), 10, replace = TRUE),
                            levels = c(1, 2),
                            labels = c("Yes", "No"))

title: Introduction to R
section: Factor levels and the reference level
text:
Factor levels and the reference level


Show the code
res <- factor(c("Urban", "Rural", "Urban"))
levels(res)        # sorted alphabetically by default: "Rural" "Urban"


[1] "Rural" "Urban"



Unless you set levels = yourself, R sorts levels alphabetically; the first level is the reference in models
Choose it deliberately: factor(x, levels = c("Urban", "Rural"))
Text in quotes is a character, not a number: mean(c("45", "52")) fails. Convert with as.numeric()

title: Introduction to R
text:
Missing values spread


Show the code
wt <- c(60, 72, NA, 58)
mean(wt)                  # NA: one unknown value makes the mean unknown


[1] NA


Show the code
mean(wt, na.rm = TRUE)    # drop the missing value for this calculation (and report it)


[1] 63.33333

title: Introduction to R
text:
Lists and Matrices


Lists

Store mixed types in one object
Can contain vectors, data frames, functions, or other lists
Good for nested results and complex outputs



Show the code
my_list <- list(name = "Alice", score = 95, data = c(1, 2, 3))



Matrices

Two-dimensional arrays with a single data type
Ideal for numeric calculations, matrices, and linear algebra
Built from vectors using matrix(), cbind(), or rbind()



Show the code
m <- matrix(1:9, nrow = 3)

title: Introduction to R
text:
Data Structures

Data frames are the most common table structure in R
They combine columns of equal length and can contain different types
Lists and matrices are also important foundational structures



Show the code
my_data <- data.frame(
  ID = 1:5,
  Name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David", "Eva"),
  Age = sample(20:50, 5, replace = TRUE)
)

by = splits the columns by group; add_overall() adds a total column.
statistic = chooses the summary: "{mean} ({sd})" for roughly symmetric variables, "{median} ({p25}, {p75})" for skewed ones.
missing_text shows how many values are missing for each variable; do not hide them.
add_p() picks a test for each variable (Wilcoxon, t-test, chi-square, Fisher) and footnotes which one.





Table 1 describes the sample; it is not where the findings go (models and effects belong in later tables).
Give n (%) for categories and mean (SD) or median (IQR) for numbers; say which in the footnote.
In a randomised trial, do not report p-values for baseline differences: any difference is by chance. Use standardised differences if you need a check.
In an observational study, p-values for exposure groups are descriptive; the size of the difference matters more than the p.
Report missing counts, and the number analysed.
Export for a paper with as_flex_table() (Word) or as_gt() (HTML/PDF).

2 groups

same rule



The default for categories is stricter than Cochran’s rule (Fisher as soon as any expected count is below 5), which is safe. The default for numbers never uses a t-test: you choose that yourself, below.










gtsummary does it
How




Welch t-test, one-way ANOVA, Welch ANOVA
add_p(test = x ~ "t.test"), "aov", "oneway.test"


Mann–Whitney, Kruskal–Wallis, Mood’s median test
"wilcox.test", "kruskal.test", "mood.test"


Chi-square (with or without Yates), Fisher, test of two proportions
"chisq.test", "chisq.test.no.correct", "fisher.test", "prop.test"


Monte Carlo p for chi-square or Fisher
test.args = x ~ list(simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)


Paired t, Wilcoxon signed-rank, McNemar
long data, "paired.t.test", "paired.wilcox.test", "mcnemar.test" with group = id


Difference with 95% CI, Cohen’s d, Hedges’ g, standardised difference (SMD)
add_difference(), test = x ~ "cohens_d", "smd"


Adjusted difference (ANCOVA), random-intercept model for clustered data
add_difference(test = x ~ "ancova", adj.vars = ...); "lme4" with group =


Confidence interval of each mean or percentage
add_ci()


Multiple-testing adjustment
add_q(method = "holm") (or "fdr")


Regression tables (linear, logistic, Cox, Poisson …)
tbl_regression(), tbl_uvregression()


Survey-weighted tests, log-rank
tbl_svysummary() + add_p(); tbl_survfit() + add_p()


Any other test
your own function in add_p(test = x ~ my_test) (example below)










Not in gtsummary (run it yourself, report it in the text or a separate table)
Use




Checking assumptions: Shapiro–Wilk, Q-Q plots, Levene
shapiro.test(), ggplot() + stat_qq(), car::leveneTest()


Repeated measures with 3 or more time points (sphericity, Greenhouse–Geisser), Friedman
rstatix::anova_test(), friedman.test()


Post hoc tests after ANOVA or Kruskal–Wallis
TukeyHSD(), rstatix::games_howell_test(), rstatix::dunn_test()


Correlation (Pearson, Spearman)
cor.test()


Effect sizes for tables and ranks: Cramér’s V, rank-biserial r, η², Kendall’s W
effectsize::cramers_v(), rstatix::wilcox_effsize(), effectsize::eta_squared()


One-sample tests against a benchmark
t.test(x, mu = 100), binom.test()


Agreement: Bland–Altman, kappa, ICC
BlandAltmanLeh, irr::kappa2(), irr::icc()






The rule, the same as in the Statistical Analysis workshop (Session 2): a number is analysed parametrically (mean (SD), t-test or Welch ANOVA) when it is roughly symmetric in every group (|skewness| < 1) and either the group has at least 30 people or, in a smaller group, Shapiro–Wilk does not reject normality; otherwise rank-based (median (IQR), Mann–Whitney or Kruskal–Wallis). A category gets chi-square when at least 80% of expected counts are ≥ 5 and none is below 1 (and, in a 2 × 2 table, none below 5); otherwise Fisher.

# One row per variable: the evidence, the decision, the test and the summary to show
choose_tests <- function(data, by, continuous, categorical) {
  k <- n_distinct(data[[by]])
  cont <- map(continuous, \(v) {
    g <- map(split(data[[v]], data[[by]]), \(x) x[!is.na(x)])
    n <- lengths(g); sk <- map_dbl(g, skewness)
    sw <- map_dbl(g, \(x) if (length(x) < 30) shapiro.test(x)$p.value else NA)
    tibble(variable = v, smallest_n = min(n), largest_skew = max(abs(sk)),
           shapiro_small_groups = if (all(is.na(sw))) NA else min(sw, na.rm = TRUE),   # NA: no group under 30
           parametric = all(abs(sk) < 1 & (n >= 30 | sw > 0.05), na.rm = TRUE))
  }) |> list_rbind() |>
    mutate(test = case_when(parametric & k == 2 ~ "t.test", parametric ~ "oneway.test",
                            k == 2 ~ "wilcox.test", TRUE ~ "kruskal.test"),
           statistic = if_else(parametric, "{mean} ({sd})", "{median} ({p25}, {p75})"))
  cat <- map(categorical, \(v) {
    e <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(table(data[[v]], data[[by]]))$expected)
    tibble(variable = v, table = paste(dim(e), collapse = " x "),
           smallest_expected = min(e), pct_below_5 = 100 * mean(e < 5),
           test = if_else((all(dim(e) == 2) & min(e) < 5) | mean(e < 5) > 0.2 | min(e) < 1,
                          "fisher.test", "chisq.test.no.correct"))
  }) |> list_rbind()
  list(continuous = cont, categorical = cat)
}

  cat <- map(categorical, \(v) {
    e <- suppressWarnings(chisq.test(table(data[[v]], data[[by]]))$expected)
    tibble(variable = v, table = paste(dim(e), collapse = " x "),
           smallest_expected = min(e), pct_below_5 = 100 * mean(e < 5),
           test = if_else((all(dim(e) == 2) & min(e) < 5) | mean(e < 5) > 0.2 | min(e) < 1,
                          "fisher.test", "chisq.test.no.correct"))
  }) |> list_rbind()
  list(continuous = cont, categorical = cat)
}

text:
Sphericity, and the correction

Sphericity: the variance of the differences is the same for every pair of time points (0–3, 0–6, 3–6)
Mauchly’s test checks it; when violated, use the Greenhouse–Geisser corrected p-value (p[GG]), which anova_test() prints alongside
Here Mauchly p < 0.001: sphericity is violated (the 0–6 month changes vary more than the 0–3), so report the GG-corrected result, ε = 0.80
ges (generalised η²) = 0.08: a modest share of the total variation, because people differ from each other far more than from one visit to the next. The F-test is huge because each person is compared with themselves


“Mean fasting glucose fell from 109.0 mg/dL at presentation to 102.8 at 3 and 98.6 at 6 months (repeated-measures ANOVA with Greenhouse–Geisser correction, F(1.61, 1012) = 659, p < 0.001; generalised η² = 0.08).”

Multiple testing

At p < 0.05, 1 in 20 tests of a true null hypothesis comes out “significant” by chance
20 independent comparisons → about a 64% chance of at least one false positive
Bonferroni: multiply each p by the number of tests (simple, strict). Holm: the same idea step by step, never worse, usually better

Expected count = row total × column total / grand total: what the table would hold if there were no association

“Diabetes was more common in adults with a past history of hypertension: 16.4% vs 3.0% (odds ratio 6.3, 95% CI 2.5 to 15.6; Fisher’s exact test, p < 0.001).”


An expected count of 2.6 triggers R’s warning “Chi-squared approximation may be incorrect”: that is the cue for Fisher
The CI is wide (2.5 to 15.6) because only 10 adults have both conditions: report it, do not hide it
This is an association, not proof that one causes the other

title: Session 3 — Categorical Outcomes
text:
Yates’ correction

chisq.test() on a 2 × 2 table applies Yates’ continuity correction by default (correct = TRUE): it subtracts 0.5 from each |observed − expected|
It makes the test conservative (p a little too large)
With adequate expected counts, correct = FALSE is fine; with small ones, use Fisher rather than relying on Yates
Whatever you choose, say which in the methods

If expected counts are too small: Monte Carlo

set.seed(2026)
chisq.test(table(p$marital_status_of_participants, p$wealth_index_of_participants),
           simulate.p.value = TRUE, B = 10000)$p.value

section: What to do with suspicious values
text:
What to do with suspicious values

Look at every variable first: summary(), a histogram, impossible combinations (SBP < DBP)
Query the source (case sheet, register) and correct what can be corrected
Decide before testing what you exclude, and report it (“4 records with SBP and DBP swapped were corrected from the case sheets”)
Run the analysis with and without the doubtful records: a sensitivity analysis


In this workshop the case sheets confirmed both errors, so they are corrected (Lab 1 does it). Every later session uses the corrected data. Extreme but possible values are not errors: they stay.

Paired or independent? Same people measured twice (before/after), or different people?
Do the assumptions hold? Roughly normal, similar spread, enough expected counts?

text:
Three numbers, not one

Effect size: how big is the difference? (difference in means, odds ratio, Cohen’s d, r)
95% confidence interval: the range of effect sizes compatible with the data
p-value: if there were truly no difference, how often would data at least this extreme turn up by chance?


A p-value is not the probability that the null hypothesis is true, and it says nothing about size or importance. p > 0.05 is not proof of no difference.

The sentence to write

“Mean weight was 64.3 kg in men and 57.3 kg in women (difference 7.0 kg, 95% CI 5.2 to 8.8; Welch t-test, p < 0.001; Cohen’s d = 0.63).”


R reports women − men (alphabetical order), a negative number: turn it round so the sentence reads naturally

Statistical Analysis Track
An elective, best after Step 1 · Basic. title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggstatsplot is an R package that combines statistical tests and publication-ready visualisations in a single function call. Each plot automatically selects, runs, and annotates the appropriate statistical test based on your data, displaying results directly on the figure.
This removes a common workflow bottleneck: running a test in one place, building a plot in another, and manually annotating results.

install.packages("ggstatsplot")

Why use it?

One function produces both the visual and the statistical result
Automatically annotates effect sizes and confidence intervals
Sensible defaults — works out of the box for most common comparisons
Output is a ggplot2 object, so you can add layers or themes as usual

A violin + boxplot combination with individual data points
The statistical test used (Welch’s ANOVA or Kruskal-Wallis, chosen automatically)
The p-value, effect size (η² or ε²), and confidence interval
Pairwise comparisons (if more than 2 groups)

Choosing parametric vs non-parametric:

# Force non-parametric (Kruskal-Wallis)
ggbetweenstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = fuel_type,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  type  = "nonparametric"   # "parametric", "nonparametric", "robust", "bayes"
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
ggscatterstats() — Correlation
Use this when you want to examine the relationship between two continuous variables.

ggscatterstats(
  data  = overall_up,
  x     = current_age,
  y     = sbp_0m,
  title = "Age vs Systolic BP at Baseline"
)

What the output shows:

A scatter plot with a linear trend line and confidence band
Pearson (or Spearman) correlation coefficient, r
p-value and 95% confidence interval for r
Marginal histograms on both axes

Using Spearman instead of Pearson:

ggscatterstats(
  data = overall_up,
  x    = current_age,
  y    = sbp_0m,
  type = "nonparametric"   # uses Spearman's rho
)

title: ggstatsplot — Introduction
text:
gghistostats() — Distribution
Use this when you want to visualise the distribution of a single continuous variable with a one-sample test.

gghistostats(
  data     = overall_up,
  x        = current_age,
  title    = "Distribution of Age at Enrolment",
  test.value = 40          # hypothesised population mean
)

What the output shows:

Histogram with overlaid density curve
One-sample t-test (or Wilcoxon signed-rank) against the specified test.value
Mean, median, and their confidence intervals

Every ggstatsplot figure includes a subtitle with the test results in a standardised format:
Welch's ANOVA, F(2, 147.3) = 5.23, p = 0.006, ω² = 0.06, 95% CI [0.01, 0.14]



Component
Meaning




Test name
Which test was used (selected automatically)


Test statistic
F, t, χ², H etc.


p-value
Statistical significance


Effect size
Practical significance (ω², d, r, etc.)


95% CI
Uncertainty around the effect size









TipInterpreting effect sizes




η² / ω²: Small ≈ 0.01, Medium ≈ 0.06, Large ≈ 0.14 (for ANOVA)
